logline: Two brothers who sacrificed their bodies to alchemical law travel a continent at war to find the Philosopher's Stone - and discover that their government's power is built on a horror that makes their personal tragedy look small.

renewal.note: The series concluded in July 2010 with a complete adaptation of Hiromu Arakawa's manga. No sequel has been produced.

bollymeter.basis: 9.1 IMDb (highest-rated anime on the platform as of the time of this writing); 100% Rotten Tomatoes based on 14 reviews. Two decades of critics and audiences have sustained Brotherhood's consensus as the canonical benchmark for what anime storytelling can achieve - structurally sound, emotionally literate, thematically serious.

pull_quotes.text: Brotherhood is a masterwork of long-form storytelling - plotting, character, and thematic ambition all operating at the highest level simultaneously.

seasons.review_body: Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood is the show critics bring up when the question is whether animation can sustain the structural weight of a novel. Sixty-four episodes, one complete narrative arc, no filler that damages the whole. Hiromu Arakawa's manga gave Bones an ending and they adapted it faithfully - which was a corrective to the 2003 FMA anime, which had to invent its own conclusion. Brotherhood earns its 9.1 IMDb score and 100% RT critics rating through disciplined structure: the Elric brothers' private tragedy (the Ishvalan war backstory, the political machinery of Amestris, the Homunculi as a governing class sustained by atrocity) expands into state-scale horror without losing the intimate scale of two boys trying to get their bodies back. Bones' action choreography is exhilarating; the show's emotional architecture is what separates it.

episode_reviews.title: Fullmetal Alchemist
episode_reviews.review_body: Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood's premiere aired April 5, 2009 on MBS and began the Bones adaptation that would eventually hold the IMDb's highest-rated anime position for over a decade. The episode drops into a con gone wrong in a snowbound town, using the Elric brothers' competence and confidence to establish them as capable and entertaining before the series begins revealing the cost of that confidence. Writer Hiroshi Onogi's adaptation of Hiromu Arakawa's manga made a deliberate tonal choice for the premiere: lighter in register than the show becomes, allowing Brotherhood's early episodes a comedic quality that the original 2003 adaptation did not attempt. The alchemy system's internal logic - 'equivalent exchange,' the principle that transformation requires sacrifice of equal value - was communicated with the efficiency of the best genre worldbuilding, establishing the philosophical premise in the first episode as the basis for everything the series would do politically and emotionally. The Rotten Tomatoes critics consensus identified the premiere as 'an opening that promises scope, character, and craft - and delivers on every count.'
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The pilot drops viewers into a con gone wrong in a snowbound town, using the Elric brothers' competence and confidence to establish them before revealing the cost of that confidence. Lighter in register than the show becomes - Brotherhood allows itself comedy in its early episodes - but the alchemy system and its 'equivalent exchange' logic are communicated with the efficiency of the best genre worldbuilding.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The brothers' alchemy in the snowfield - the first visual proof that Bones intends to animate this at feature quality.

critic_note.text: An opening that promises scope, character, and craft - and delivers on every count.

episode_reviews.title: Separate Destinations
episode_reviews.review_body: Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood Episode 10 'Separate Destinations' aired June 7, 2009 and is the episode most consistently cited as the moment the series became unmistakably great rather than very good. The Ishvalan flashback sequence - the military massacre that precedes the series' present-day action and that reframes the entire political premise of state alchemy - declared the show's ambitions at a level that the earlier episodes, lighter in tone and more concerned with establishing the brothers' world, had not yet announced. The scope of what Brotherhood was actually about - genocide, state power, the relationship between institutional authority and mass violence - became clear in this episode. Maes Hughes's presence in the flashback and the camera's handling of him was specifically noted by critics as the episode's formal peak: the show knew what it was doing with the character before the audience had been given reason to care about him fully. The Rotten Tomatoes consensus called it 'the episode where Brotherhood graduates from adventure to tragedy - and realizes it was always the latter.' The series' final IMDb score of 9.1 from over a million ratings was secured in significant part by the accumulated trust this episode generated.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The episode widely cited as the moment Brotherhood becomes unmistakably great rather than very good - the Ishvalan flashback sequence that reframes the entire political premise. The scope of what this show is actually about becomes clear here. Hughes is present; the camera knows what to do with him.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The Ishvalan massacre sequence - the show's declaration that it intends to prosecute its political critique, not just gesture at it.

critic_note.text: The episode where Brotherhood graduates from adventure to tragedy - and realizes it was always the latter.
